claims.text: Adaptive free-energy integration combining enhanced umbrella sampling with dynamic reweighting can capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions in both solid and fluid phases.
The proposed method can reduce computational cost while retaining ab initio-level fidelity near fusion.
The method is applicable to elemental metals, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Adaptive umbrella sampling can target critical regions of configurational space, including high-barrier and rare-event regions.
Reweighting can reconstruct phase free energies while retaining all relevant entropy contributions.
Enhanced sampling of key configurational regions ensures accurate reconstruction of free-energy surfaces.
Accurate reconstruction through enhanced sampling preserves detailed entropy contributions.
Selectively sampling configurations that contribute most strongly to the free-energy difference is sufficient to accelerate the calculation.
Adaptive umbrella sampling identifies critical configurational regions early in a simulation.
Dynamic reweighting can reconstruct full free-energy landscapes including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
Strategic sampling reduces the number of molecular-dynamics steps required relative to conventional methods.
The proposed method will reproduce explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy results within approximately 5% error.
The proposed method may reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will substantially outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluation is accurate but computationally expensive.
The computational expense of existing free-energy workflows is particularly severe for high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis applies to metallic systems at high temperatures up to the fusion point.

contradictions.description: The initial-state description includes temperatures near or above fusion, whereas the boundary limits applicability to temperatures up to the fusion point. This leaves the intended liquid-state temperature range internally inconsistent.
